seoTitle: How to Use TradingView Replay for Free
metaDescription: Learn how to use TradingView's free Bar Replay feature to practice trading, replay historical candles, and test entries and exits without risk.
intro: TradingView's Bar Replay feature lets you rewind a chart and watch price unfold candle by candle, which is a great free way to practice trading strategies without risking real money. It's tucked into the regular chart toolbar rather than hidden behind a paid plan, so anyone can use it once they know where to look. This guide covers finding the Replay button, starting a replay session on a real chart, and stepping through candles the way you would while practicing entries and exits.

steps.heading: Find the Replay button on your chart
steps.body: On any chart — this example uses the Dow Jones Industrial Average Index through Capital.com — the top toolbar includes Indicators, an Alert button, and Replay sitting right next to it. The chart also shows the usual live-market layout: a watchlist on the right with major indices and stocks, buy and sell price boxes in the top left, and a volume histogram beneath the candles. None of that changes when you switch into replay mode — you're working with the same interface, just controlling time within it.

image.caption: A live TradingView chart with the Replay button in the toolbar, next to Indicators and Alert.

steps.heading: Click Replay and pick your starting bar
steps.body: Clicking Replay changes the toolbar — Select bar becomes the active instruction, along with playback controls: a rewind-to-start button, play/pause, a speed selector currently at 1x, and a skip-to-end button. Click directly on the chart at the candle where you want the replay to begin; everything after that point disappears from view until you play or step forward, which is what makes this useful for practicing a decision without your eye jumping ahead to see what happened next.

image.caption: Replay mode active with the Select bar control and playback buttons — rewind, play, speed, and skip to end.

steps.heading: Step through candles and watch a ghost "Replay" watermark
steps.body: Once you're replaying, TradingView stamps a faint "Replay" watermark across the middle of the chart so it's always visually obvious you're not looking at live data. The volume bars and price scale keep updating exactly as they would live, and the price boxes in the top left track whatever candle you've stepped to, not the actual current market price. This is the point where you'd place simulated trades against the chart as it plays forward, exactly as you would in a live session.

image.caption: A replay session mid-playback, with the translucent Replay watermark confirming you're viewing historical candles, not live data.

steps.heading: Practice entries, exits, and stop placement
steps.body: With the chart paused at your chosen bar, place a simulated entry the way you would on a live trade — mark where you'd enter, where your stop loss would sit, and your take-profit target — then click play or step forward one candle at a time to see how price actually developed. The value here is emotional as much as technical: replay forces you to make a decision without knowing the outcome, which is the part live paper trading on a moving chart can't fully replicate since you can always just wait and watch instead of committing.

steps.heading: Use the speed control to fit your practice style
steps.body: The 1x speed setting next to the play button can be adjusted if you want candles to advance faster once you're comfortable reacting quickly, or you can rely entirely on manual stepping if you'd rather deliberate over every bar. New traders generally get more out of manual, one-candle-at-a-time stepping early on, since it forces a full read of the setup before moving on, while faster playback is better once you're testing how a strategy performs across a longer stretch of history.

steps.heading: Avoid the most common replay mistake
steps.body: The single easiest way to defeat the purpose of Bar Replay is scrolling or dragging the chart forward to peek at candles that haven't played yet before making your decision. It's tempting, especially when a setup looks ambiguous, but doing it regularly trains you to trade with information you'll never actually have live. Treat the edge of the visible candles as a hard wall the same way you would in real time.

steps.heading: Combine replay with journaling for real improvement
steps.body: Replay sessions are most useful when you write down each simulated trade — entry, stop, target, and reasoning — the same way you'd log a live trade, then review afterward whether your read of the setup was accurate. Running replay without any record of your decisions turns it into passive chart-watching rather than deliberate practice, and the free version gives you enough historical range on most symbols to build a meaningful practice log before ever risking real capital.

faq.question: Is TradingView Bar Replay really free?
faq.answer: Yes, Bar Replay is available on TradingView's free plan and appears right in the standard chart toolbar next to Indicators and Alert, with no separate purchase needed.

faq.question: Can I use Bar Replay with Paper Trading?
faq.answer: Yes, combining Bar Replay with Paper Trading lets you simulate trades on historical price action for realistic practice, including stop loss and take profit placement.

faq.question: Does Bar Replay work on all symbols?
faq.answer: Bar Replay generally works across most symbols with available historical data, including indices like the Dow Jones shown in a typical replay session, though exact history length can vary by asset.

faq.question: What's the biggest mistake beginners make with replay mode?
faq.answer: A common mistake is scrolling or dragging ahead to see what happens before making a trading decision, which removes the realistic, no-peeking practice value entirely.

faq.question: How do I know I'm in replay mode and not looking at a live chart?
faq.answer: TradingView stamps a translucent "Replay" watermark across the middle of the chart during a replay session, so it's always clear you're viewing historical candles rather than live data.
